analysis.one_liner: Loosens Clean Air Act rules so many power plant upgrades no longer trigger modern pollution controls.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House subcommittee on a 13-9 vote but never received a vote in the full committee or the House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill changes how the Clean Air Act decides when an upgrade to a power plant or factory counts as a "modification." Under it, a change would only trigger requirements to install modern pollution controls if the plant's maximum hourly emissions rate rose above both its original design rate and the highest hourly rate it actually hit in the previous 10 years. That means a plant could run longer hours each year and emit more total pollution without adding new controls, as long as its hourly rate stayed the same. The bill was introduced in June 2017, moved through a House subcommittee in July 2018, and died without a vote in the full committee or the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Operators of older coal-fired and other fossil-fueled power plants and industrial facilities. If the bill became law, they could upgrade or change how they run plants without triggering New Source Review, the Clean Air Act process that would otherwise require them to install up-to-date pollution controls on older units.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes a new rule into the Clean Air Act: a physical change or change in operations counts as increasing pollution only if the plant's maximum achievable hourly emissions rate rises above both its original design rate and the highest hourly rate actually achieved in the prior 10 years.

Supporters argue the existing rules penalize plants for improving efficiency or reliability, since routine changes can force expensive retrofit requirements; the bill would let plants make changes based on their hourly emissions rate instead.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near and downwind of older power plants and industrial facilities. Because the test is based on hourly emissions rates, a plant that emits the same amount per hour but runs many more hours a year would emit more total pollution each year without being required to install modern controls.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near and downwind of plants

drawbacks.text: The bill measures pollution as a maximum hourly rate, so a plant that runs longer hours would emit more total pollution each year while escaping the requirement to add modern pollution controls.

Older plants that avoid upgrades would keep emitting at older, dirtier technology levels, shifting cleanup costs onto the surrounding public in the form of air pollution rather than onto the plant's operator.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes almost entirely to operators of older fossil-fueled plants, who would avoid the cost of installing modern pollution controls during upgrades. The cost is increased total air pollution from plants that run more hours, borne by nearby and downwind residents in health impacts. The bill's supporters frame it as removing a barrier to plant modernization, but the bill does not pair that flexibility with any substitute protection for air quality.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee for a year and a half; a subcommittee advanced it in July 2018, but the full committee and the House never voted on it, and the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. H. Morgan Griffith introduced the bill on June 29, 2017, joined by Reps. McKinley and Jenkins of West Virginia, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment on June 30, 2017.
The subcommittee held a markup session on July 17, 2018, and forwarded an amended version to the full committee on a 13-9 vote.
The bill gathered 20 cosponsors, 19 Republicans and 1 Democrat.
The full Energy and Commerce Committee never marked up the bill and the House never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who live near and downwind of older fossil-fueled power plants are better off, since the current, stricter rules still apply. The bill's target audience, operators of aging coal-fired plants, gained nothing; they remain subject to existing Clean Air Act modification rules.

industries.industry: Coal-fired and other fossil-fuel electric utilities
industries.note: The bill would let these operators upgrade or extend the running hours of aging plants without triggering requirements to install modern pollution controls, because the test is based on hourly emissions rates rather than total annual pollution. Their cost savings come as added air pollution for nearby and downwind communities.

industries.industry: Industrial facility operators subject to Clean Air Act permitting
industries.note: Any stationary source could change equipment or operations as long as its maximum hourly emissions rate did not exceed historical highs, avoiding costly control-technology retrofits. The public bears the resulting increase in total annual emissions.

industries.industry: Pollution-control equipment and environmental compliance industries
industries.note: Fewer plant changes qualifying as modifications means fewer mandated installations of scrubbers, filters, and monitoring equipment, and less demand for the compliance work tied to New Source Review reviews.
